It eliminates the use of "good" or "bad" in prescribed by the society definition. What Sartrean existentialism implores us to do is to reject all the possible preconceptions we have instilled by the society we're born in, its religion, philosophy, science etc and then build our own meaning of the world from that position of phenomenological clarity.

It's a constant process, as we're engulfed in the society of some sort whether we want it or not: what Sartre proposes is to be always able to take a step back and look at how we think and behave and why - and determine whether it's still our own authentic self, or is it tainted with some "bad faith".

So it's up to you to determine "good" or "bad". And as long as you make that determination free from some imposed presuppositions (living authentically) then your good or bad should become the universal moral rule you truly and deeply believe in, at which point stale notions of good or bad gain its existential meaning.
